headline: I am currently serving as the 14th seal on a single exam paper, and I haven't seen my family in three weeks
body:
My name is Rajesh, and until last month, I was a perfectly happy junior clerk. Now, I am officially classified as 'Human Lockbox #4' in the Education Ministry’s new four-tier security protocol. My job is to sit in a climate-controlled vault in a basement in Delhi, physically hugging a sealed envelope containing the mathematics paper for a competitive exam until the exact minute of the test. I am not allowed to eat, sleep, or even sneeze, because apparently, a sneeze is now considered a 'Tier 2 security breach'.

They told me this was a temporary measure to prevent leaks, but the paperwork I signed says my tenure lasts until the next assessment cycle, which is in 2028. My colleagues, Locks #1 through #3, are currently stationed in secret locations across the country—one is inside a submarine off the coast of Goa, and another is supposedly living inside a hollowed-out pillar at a railway station. We communicate only through coded taps on the wall that must be approved by three separate parliamentary committees.

Yesterday, my supervisor poked his head through the vault air-vent to ask if I’d noticed any leaks. I tried to tell him that my leg had gone numb three days ago and that I’m starting to develop a strange, telepathic bond with the algebraic equations inside the envelope, but he just marked my clipboard as 'Compliant' and sealed the vent back up with industrial-grade wax. I honestly don't even care who wins the exam anymore; I just want to know if, at the end of this, I’m allowed to keep the envelope as a souvenir or if I have to be incinerated along with the scratch paper.
caption: Meet the man whose job security is literal, not professional. Are the four tiers of protection enough, or do we need a fifth human seal? #EducationReform #ExamSecurity #BureaucracyLife (satire)
igHook: Would you volunteer for this if it meant a government pension?
imagePrompt: A dimly lit, cramped concrete room featuring a single wooden chair placed in the center, with a small stack of official-looking, wax-sealed manila envelopes resting on a desk nearby.
